content.text: Chapter Five
The Prince’s Seal
They reached the forward command post two hours after nightfall, with the rain at their backs and the smoke of the burned way station still caught in their cloaks.

The post occupied a fortified lodge where Eversong’s last tended road met the first blighted trees. Gold leaves clung to the branches north of the palisade. Beyond its southern ditch, the forest stood bare beneath a low green haze. Farstriders had filled the space between with wet tents, arrow crates, tethered hawkstriders, and braziers whose ward-flames hissed whenever the wind changed.

Healers took Theron at the gate despite his objections. Lethira surrendered the recovered maps but kept Serenya’s black-fletched arrow. Rynel crossed the yard without assistance. Only Falanaras, walking half a pace behind him, saw the captain’s left boot drag twice through the mud.
Rynel straightened before the command lodge. By the time the sentries opened the door, fatigue had disappeared behind the severe economy of his bearing.

Ranger-General Halduron Brightwing waited over a long table beneath three hanging lamps. Two Farstrider officers stood beside him, along with a magister in a crimson mantle. A map of the southern border covered the table. The markers upon it ended well north of where the day’s fighting had taken place.
Halduron looked over Theron’s new bindings, the black stains on Rynel’s gauntlets, and the blood dried along Lethira’s sleeve. “Report.”

Rynel gave it without ornament. They had followed the stolen supplies to the ruined relay station, found the Scourge rebuilding its buried command focus, destroyed two linked forces, recovered the ward-stone fragments, and burned what remained. He named their injuries and omitted his own.
“You destroyed a column of that size with four soldiers?” Halduron asked.
“No,” Rynel said. “We arrived while an Argent Dawn patrol was already engaged.”
Halduron’s hand stopped above the map. “Argent forces crossed into Quel’Thalas without notice.”

“Six paladins pursuing the same remnant from the Plaguelands,” Rynel said. “Their commander acknowledged the border and claimed no authority over it. Two died before we reached them. The others withdrew south with their wounded.”
“A border whose markers are ash remains a border.” Halduron shifted one of the map weights south. “I will send Light’s Hope a notice. Courtesy can arrive after their soldiers, if it must.”
His gaze moved to Falanaras. “You knew one of them.”
Falanaras had not expected that detail to reach the report. “Edric Hale. We were friends before the war. He is attached to the Dawn from Stormwind.”
Halduron studied him for a heartbeat, then returned to Rynel. “You said a second force entered from the southeast. Who was behind it?”
Lethira laid the black arrow across the map. “Dark Rangers. Five of them. Serenya Duskrunner led the patrol.”
The room became still in a different way. Halduron did not touch the arrow. “I remember Duskrunner.”
“She remembers us,” Lethira said. Her voice gave nothing away. “Her scouts were following the reinforcement from the south. They killed both necromancers and helped bring down the abomination.”
“Under whose orders?”
“She named the Forsaken,” Rynel said. “No commander. No demand. She gave us a Scourge route leading toward Deatholme and the location of a culvert used to avoid the Scar.”
Halduron looked from the arrow to the marked leather Lethira had brought. “Sylvanas does not spend rangers without purpose. Useful aid does not make its purpose ours.”
“It kept twelve more Scourge from reaching the relay,” Rynel said.
“Then it was useful.” Halduron’s attention sharpened. “You mentioned a standoff after the fighting.”

Theron answered from the chair a healer had forced upon him. “The paladins objected to the Dark Rangers. The Dark Rangers objected to being objected to. Their commander reminded everyone that Forsaken serve elsewhere in the Dawn and ordered weapons down.”
“And they obeyed?” Halduron asked.
“Eventually,” Lethira said.

Halduron exhaled through his nose. “Six unannounced paladins, five Forsaken rangers, and four blood elves with no reinforcement. I would prefer the next border incident to contain fewer claims upon my attention.” He held out his hand. “The command focus.”
Rynel placed a splinter of black crystal in his palm. The magister raised a warded cloth to receive it. A faint green current crawled over the captain’s fingers before releasing them.
Halduron saw the current. He also saw the tremor that followed. “How much did you take from it?”
“Enough to break its hold,” Rynel said.

It answered the wording and nothing beneath it. Falanaras watched Halduron recognize the evasion. Before the Ranger-General could press, boots struck the outer corridor at a pace barely short of running.

A young Farstrider entered with rain shining on his shoulders. He carried a narrow case of red lacquer bound with silver wire. The wax impressed over its clasp bore the sunburst seal of House Sunstrider.
Every person in the room straightened. “Message relayed from Silvermoon,” the ranger said. He looked at Halduron, then Rynel. “It came through the southern route. From Outland.”

Outland had existed in Falanaras’s mind as reports, promises, and the distant place where Kael’thas sought salvation for his people. The word displaced the rain, the border, even Serenya’s arrow. Halduron broke the wax and read in silence before passing the inner sheet to Rynel.

“His Highness requests reinforcements for an operation of decisive importance,” Halduron said. “Its purpose is withheld until the company reaches Outland. Captain Starweaver is named among the officers requested. The company gathers in Silvermoon within ten days.”

Pride rose in Falanaras before caution could touch it. Then Rynel’s hand trembled against the parchment. Halduron lowered his voice. “You may decline on grounds of current duty or health. I will send that answer under my authority.” Rynel folded the message. “Deatholme first.” “You have no Deatholme assignment yet,” Halduron said. “You have one full day inside this camp. Brightshield will remain with the healers. The rest of you will eat, sleep, and report here at first light the day after tomorrow. That is an order, Captain.” After a moment, Rynel answered, “Understood.”
Halduron kept his word. No field order reached them for the whole of the next day.

Theron slept beneath the healers’ supervision after they rebound his ribs. Lethira spent an hour giving a Farstrider scribe the exact placement of every altered trail sign, then took her bedroll to the loft above the hawkstrider stable. Falanaras washed Scourge matter from his glaive, ate without tasting the meal, and slept until the afternoon bells.

Rynel accepted a cot in the officers’ room. When Falanaras passed its open door near midday, the captain lay fully dressed with one forearm across his eyes. A measured crystal sat untouched on the stool beside him. The sight should have been reassuring. It was not.

Near dusk, Falanaras climbed the northern firing step. Eversong shone beyond the road in wet gold. When he turned south, the same rain vanished into the dark canopy of the Ghostlands. The post stood between the two landscapes as if a palisade and fifty tired soldiers could keep one from becoming the other.

Lethira joined him, turning the black arrow between her fingers. Below them, Theron emerged from the infirmary with the careful posture of a man determined to make pain look ceremonial. None of them spoke about Edric, Serenya, or Outland. Rest had given each subject more room rather than less.

After sunset, Rynel found them at the cook tent. He had shaved and changed his blood-stiffened undertunic. His hands were steady around the bowl. “Command lodge at first light,” he said. “Bring field kit.”

The muddy magister waited with Halduron the next morning. When he touched the recovered crystal splinter, a sick green thread rose from it and spread across the map in branching lines. Several converged on Deatholme. Others reached toward abandoned sanctums, grave pits, and stretches of the Dead Scar where patrols had vanished.

“The stronghold is coordinating its outer remnants through linked anchors,” the magister said. “The fragment refers to an administrative register below the eastern ruins. It should identify the anchor sites, their garrisons, and the command routes between them.”

“The Scourge will alter those routes when the missing column fails to report,” Halduron said. “We may have two days. I can assign another unit.” Rynel pointed to the eastern wall. “Another unit would need time to study the focus. Valeflame can reach this approach unseen. Dawnspear can read the command currents. Brightshield can keep the passage open.” Halduron’s gaze settled on him. “And you?” “I correct their errors.”

Lethira looked down. Theron’s expression did not move. Halduron let the silence stand before he said, “You leave after breakfast. If any one of you believes the captain cannot continue, you withdraw. The same applies if Brightshield’s ribs open, if Valeflame loses the route, or if Dawnspear cannot break the outer ward. No objective in Deatholme is worth four soldiers I cannot replace.”

They prepared in the wet yard. Theron selected a heavier shield. Lethira blackened the bright fittings on her bow. Falanaras sealed copies of the ward sequence beneath the oiled flap of his pack while Rynel tucked the Sunstrider message case beneath his cloak. The captain divided their crystals with an apothecary’s exactness, giving six to each of them and keeping four. When Falanaras challenged the count, Rynel tied his pouch shut. “Keep your allotment.” Farstriders saluted as they passed through the gate. Rynel acknowledged them and led his unit south.

The road failed by degrees. Laid stone gave way to cracked paving, then to two muddy tracks divided by thorn. They avoided the Dead Scar and moved through blighted woodland where pale fungi climbed the trunks. Once, a flock of carrion birds burst from the branches ahead. Lethira vanished into the brush before the last wingbeat faded and returned to report three ghouls worrying at a stag. They circled east without drawing steel.
Rynel maintained a measured pace. He did not stumble. Each time the ground rose, however, his left hand settled near the pouch at his belt. It never opened the flap.

At dusk they sheltered in the remains of a wayside shrine. The image within had lost its face and most of one arm, though a few chips of blue enamel still clung to the robe. Someone had scratched the new name of their people across the old dedication. The letters were crude and deep: SIN’DOREI.
Theron lowered himself against the wall. “If Outland has beds, I volunteer.”
“You volunteer whenever furniture is mentioned,” Lethira said.
“A soldier should understand his strengths.”

Rynel took first watch. Falanaras sat beside him in the roofless doorway while Lethira and Theron rested. Beyond the shrine, the trees stood black against a dim green haze rising from the south. Deatholme lay past those ridges. Its fires stained the low clouds on nights when the wind turned.
“Why did he name you?” Falanaras asked.
Rynel turned the lacquered message case in his hands. He had carried it beneath his cloak all day. “I served with one of the prince’s household officers before the war. He knew my record.”
“That is all?”
“It is sufficient.” Rynel slipped the case back beneath his cloak. “Secret operations favor soldiers whose records are longer than their questions.”
“Halduron offered to refuse for you.”

“Halduron offered to let me live with having refused.” The captain’s profile remained still against the southern haze. “Our prince asks for soldiers while he searches for an answer to what we have become. If I am fit to serve here, I am fit to answer him.”

Falanaras heard the flaw and understood why Rynel needed it to remain unspoken. Fitness had become a door that opened both ways. Deny it here, and the captain surrendered his command. Claim it here, and he could not decline Outland without admitting fear.
“Your number?” Falanaras asked.

Rynel’s gaze shifted to him. For years, the question had belonged to the captain. Recruits answered because discipline required truth before pride. Hearing it returned seemed to cost him more than anger would have.
“Four,” he said at last.
It was the first time Falanaras had heard Rynel answer the question with a number.

He took one shard from his own pouch and held it out. Rynel looked at the green glow for several breaths, then accepted it. He drew slowly. The light faded without the violent flare Falanaras had begun to dread.
“Three,” Rynel said, returning the spent crystal.
“Then keep watch.”
The corner of the captain’s mouth tightened. “Sleep while the privilege remains available.”

They broke camp before first light. Mist filled the low ground and left the ridges exposed like islands of black root and stone. Rynel walked at the front with Lethira, studying the copied route whenever the trees concealed the southern haze. Falanaras followed with Theron, close enough to hear the captain’s breathing whenever the path climbed.

For the first hour, no one spoke. The forest supplied its own uneasy company: water dripping from bare branches, carrion beetles clicking beneath the bark, something heavy moving parallel to them beyond sight. Falanaras kept one hand near his glaive and felt the lacquered message case ahead of him as keenly as any hidden threat.
Theron glanced toward Rynel. “The message named him, not us.”
“I know,” Falanaras said.
“He will answer it if he leaves Deatholme alive.”
Lethira looked back over one shoulder. “An ambitious condition.”
Falanaras watched the captain’s measured stride. “He should not make the journey alone.”
“The prince requested officers and reinforcements,” Rynel said without turning. “Silvermoon will choose them. You will not volunteer yourself into sealed orders.”
“We were discussing whether you could reach Silvermoon without falling over,” Lethira said.
Rynel stepped over a fallen branch. “Discuss it more quietly.”
Lethira glanced toward Falanaras. “His hearing remains fit.”

The exchange did not loosen the pressure in Falanaras’s chest. Rynel spoke as though the decision belonged wholly to command, yet the lacquered case traveled at the center of their formation like another wounded man. If the captain reached Silvermoon, Kael’thas’s summons would carry him beyond Quel’Thalas while his control was failing. Falanaras could not imagine allowing that journey. He had no rank with which to prevent it and no order permitting him to follow.

He tried to imagine passing beyond Azeroth. His mind supplied no alien sky or shattered land, only Kael’thas as he remained in public memory: bright-haired beneath a sweeping crimson mantle and a high red-gold shoulder guard, with three fiery Verdant Spheres circling above him as he named the survivors sin’dorei and promised that their suffering would lead somewhere other than extinction. Falanaras had built years of service upon that promise without ever expecting it to reach into his own life.
“Would you go?” Theron asked quietly.
Falanaras knew he was being offered the dignity of treating the question as hypothetical. “Yes.”
“For the prince?”
Falanaras watched Rynel’s shoulders move beneath the dark cloak. “For what he may have found. For the captain. I do not know which answer I would give first.”
Theron accepted that with a nod. “Then the honest answer is both.”

The path narrowed along a slope where the soil had slumped away. Rynel stopped before the crossing and removed the message case from beneath his cloak. His hand shook once as he held it toward Falanaras.
“Your pack is better sealed,” the captain said.

The claim was plausible enough to preserve them both. Falanaras tucked the case beneath the oiled flap beside the copied ward sequences. The prince’s seal rested between orders taken from the Scourge, each document pointing toward a different war.
They saw Deatholme near midday.

The stronghold occupied the southern horizon in broken towers and blackened walls. Once, the site had guarded roads through living forest. The Scourge had enlarged it with timber palisades, bone scaffolds, and siegeworks sunk into poisoned earth. Smoke dragged from its chimneys. Winged shapes circled above the central ruin, too large to be birds.
Falanaras had fought within sight of Deatholme before. Proximity had never made it seem less obscene. The place endured with the patience of a wound that had learned to feed itself.

They left the last trail and crawled through dead bracken toward the eastern wall. Lethira led, choosing ground where exposed roots broke their outlines. Twice she stopped them with a closed fist. The first patrol passed thirty paces ahead: six armored corpses behind a floating crystal lantern whose green beam swept the trees. The second consisted of ghouls driven by an acolyte in stitched robes. Its chant made Falanaras’s teeth ache before he could hear the words.
Rynel’s breathing changed when the acolyte came near. One slow intake. A held pause. His fingers pressed into the mud.
Falanaras laid two fingers against the captain’s wrist. Rynel did not look at him. The patrol passed. When the chant faded, he withdrew his hand and gestured them forward.

The entry lay beneath a collapsed watch post where runoff had cut a channel under the foundations. Old drainage stones formed a passage barely high enough to crawl through. The Scourge had sealed it with a ward instead of rubble. Five hooked runes hung in the darkness, each turning at a different pace.
Falanaras studied the sequence copied from the focus. “The third rune listens outward. The others carry its report inward.”
“Can you blind it?” Theron whispered.
“For a breath.”
“Take two,” Rynel said. “It is a generous fortress.”

Falanaras set his glaive against the stones and reached for the ward. Necromantic current slid along the crescent blade, cold enough to numb his palms. He caught the listening rune between one pulse and the next, twisted its attention toward the empty woods, and held. Lethira went first, then Theron. Rynel entered behind them. By the time Falanaras dragged himself through, the false report was fraying. He released it and the five runes resumed their turning.

The passage descended through wet stone. They crawled until the smell of rain vanished beneath old blood, lamp grease, and the dust of opened graves. Farther in, the drain widened into a service corridor. Iron hooks lined the walls. Several still held scraps of yellowed parchment, as if the place had once been used for stores before its keepers found another purpose for the shelves.
Lethira raised one hand. Voices murmured beyond the next turn.

They waited in darkness while two acolytes crossed the adjoining hall. One carried a stack of ledgers chained together through their spines. The other bore a shallow bowl in which three severed fingers twitched and pointed toward different passages. Neither looked into the service corridor.
When they had gone, Rynel touched the wall. A low green pulse answered beneath his palm.
“The anchor current runs through the masonry,” he said. “The register will be near its strongest branch.”
“Can you follow it?” Falanaras asked.
Rynel removed his hand. Green remained in the lines of his palm before his gauntlet closed over it. “Yes.”
The lower vault had once been an archive.

Stone shelves rose along its walls, crowded with worm-eaten rolls and iron document cases. A long table occupied the center. The Scourge had driven copper stakes through its surface and stretched a hide map between them. Black threads connected marked sites across the Ghostlands. Each thread descended through the map into a stone beneath the table, where power beat with a slow, malignant rhythm.

Three acolytes worked around it. One read figures from a chained ledger. Another moved bone markers across the hide. The third stood with both hands spread above the buried stone, feeding a whispered command into the network. Beside the far door waited what the Scourge called a deathguard: an elven corpse riveted into tarnished plate, held unnaturally upright by iron braces along its spine. Shrunken gray skin clung to the exposed half of its face. One eye socket was empty; the other held a pinprick of corpse-light. Runes cut into its jaw and breastbone glimmered through gaps in the armor, each mark bound to the two-handed sword across its knees. It sat without breath or motion, but both gauntleted hands already enclosed the hilt.
The four blood elves watched through a gap where the archive door no longer met its frame.

Lethira pointed to the acolyte at the anchor, then to the reader. Two arrows. Theron indicated the deathguard and raised his shield a fraction. Rynel gave Falanaras the table and the third acolyte. He held up three fingers, preparing the count.
The anchor pulsed.
Power moved through the wall and across Falanaras’s skin. The hunger behind his teeth sharpened at once. Beside him, Rynel stopped breathing.
One finger lowered.
A second pulse entered the room. The acolyte’s chant rose with it. Rynel leaned toward the sound. His lips parted, and the tendons in his neck drew taut.
Falanaras caught his wrist.
Rynel tore free and entered the vault before the count was finished.

The first acolyte turned. Rynel seized the front of its robes and struck one gauntleted hand against its chest. Instead of breaking the spell, he dragged it straight into himself. Green light burst between them. The acolyte screamed as its working ripped backward through its body and poured into the captain’s arm. Its skin collapsed against the hollows of its face. Rynel flung the corpse aside and reached for the next source before it struck the floor.

Lethira’s arrow took the chanting acolyte through the shoulder instead of the throat. The broken count had spoiled her shot. Its command tore loose from the anchor and lashed across the chamber. Falanaras caught the current on his glaive. Pain burned from his palms to his elbows as he forced it down into the floor.
The deathguard rose.

Theron met its sword with his shield. The impact drove him back through the doorway, boots gouging dust from the stones. His bandaged side struck the frame. He grunted, reset his stance, and caught the next blow before it reached Lethira.

The third acolyte sent a fork of shadow at Rynel. He opened his hand. The spell bent toward him, gathered into a narrow stream, and vanished beneath his skin. His back arched. For an instant Falanaras saw relief cross the captain’s face with the terrible intimacy of pleasure witnessed by accident.
Then Rynel pulled harder.

The acolyte’s spell failed. Its wards followed, peeling away in strips of green-black radiance. Rynel continued to draw after there was no working left to seize. Light streamed from the runes sewn into its robes, from the charms at its throat, from its eyes and open mouth. His shoulders curved toward the flow. His free hand opened and closed beside it, fingers hooked around nothing.
“Captain!” Falanaras shouted.
Rynel did not hear him.
The wounded chanter clawed at the copper stake nearest its hand. A red spark traveled down the black thread beneath it.
Falanaras abandoned the current on his glaive and crossed the room. He struck the acolyte’s wrist aside, but one bent finger brushed the stake.
The anchor-stone awakened beneath the table.

A bell sounded with no metal behind it. The note passed through flesh and stone. Black threads snapped taut across the hide map, carrying crimson sparks outward toward every marked site. From somewhere above came the answer: chains dropping, doors slamming open, the first distant howl of an alarm moving through Deatholme.
The deathguard forced Theron to one knee. Lethira put an arrow through the rune carved in its jaw. Bone splintered. The construct’s head snapped sideways, but its sword remained raised.

Falanaras drove the crescent of his glaive beneath the deathguard’s breastplate. The blade crossed the runes feeding its sword arm, and power ripped out through the wound. Cold fire burst between the iron braces as the magical loss became damage inside the corpse. A second working still hardened the two-handed sword and drove strength through its grip. Falanaras hooked that completed enchantment free and cast it across the room. Blue-green force closed around Theron’s shield arm instead. He rose behind the stolen strength and struck with the iron rim. The deathguard toppled across the table, tearing copper stakes from the hide. Lethira’s second arrow entered the exposed cavity in its chest. The remaining runes went dark.
Rynel still held the last acolyte upright. With his body bowed around the failing glow, the hard planes of his face had sharpened into hollows. His eyes burned too brightly beneath his brow.
Falanaras struck his forearm with the haft of the glaive. Once. Twice. On the third blow, Rynel’s grip broke. The acolyte fell, robes smoking where the captain had touched them.
Rynel turned on Falanaras with green fire gathered in his hand. His shoulders remained hunched and his chin thrust forward, stripped for one terrible instant of every posture that made him a captain.
Lethira drew on him. Theron stepped between them, shield dented and blood spreading through the binding at his side.
“Captain,” Theron said.
Nothing in his voice pleaded. The title carried years of obedience, training yards, failed walls, shared watch, and all the fallen they had left behind.

Rynel looked at the fire in his hand. His fingers closed. The glow leaked between them, diminished, and went out. His gaze followed the last thread of it with naked craving before he forced his eyes toward Theron.
Lethira lowered her bow by inches.
The alarm continued above them. Heavy feet entered a distant stairwell. The anchor under the table answered with another pulse. Rynel flinched, and his head turned toward it before he caught himself.
“Report,” he said. His voice was raw, though the command within it held.
Theron pressed one hand to his ribs. “Bruised pride. Open wound. Shield remains offensive to look at.”
“Valeflame?”
“I have six arrows less than I wanted and one more target than I expected.” She did not specify the target. “Fit to move.”

Rynel faced Falanaras last. The change was impossible to hide now. His shoulders had drawn forward; his cheeks looked hollow beneath overbright eyes; the fingers around his burned palm remained hooked after the fire was gone. Falanaras remembered the Wretched he had dragged from a Murder Row cellar, jaw slack and all higher thought narrowed to the nearest glow. Rynel had not crossed that final distance. He stood near enough for Falanaras to see it. “Dawnspear?”

Falanaras wanted to say unfit. Halduron’s order gave him the authority. The word waited behind his teeth while he looked at the emptied acolytes, Theron’s blood, and Lethira’s bow. Rynel had fed beyond need, beyond orders, and nearly turned on them when interrupted. He also stood between the team and the approaching undead, forcing his body back into a soldier’s bearing with whatever discipline remained.
“Fit to move,” Falanaras said. “After we take what we came for.”
Something passed through Rynel’s expression—gratitude, shame, or anger denied a proper object. “Then move.”

Falanaras seized the chained ledgers from the floor and cut through their links. Lethira found a lacquered map case beneath the dead reader’s robes. Inside lay a narrow plan of Deatholme’s lower passages, marked with the same black threads as the hide map. Several lines met at anchors set beneath gates and stairs. One continued east through a service route that emerged beyond the outer wall.
Their entrance lay north of them. The alarm marks had already turned red along that passage.
“The drain is lost,” Lethira said.

Falanaras opened the first ledger. Columns of sites and symbols filled its pages. The register they needed was referenced beside a seal stamped deeper in the understructure. The copied line named a primary anchor and a control archive beyond the old ossuary stairs.
Their evidence had shown them the network. The command register lay farther inside it.
Another howl rose beyond the vault door. This one was close enough that dust sifted from the lintel.

Rynel picked up his glaive. The movement brought him upright by force. Green light moved beneath the skin of his throat, too bright in the gaunt hollows above his gorget. “We follow the anchor line to the control archive. From there, we take the eastern route out.”
“Deeper,” Theron said.
“Yes.” Rynel’s gaze caught on the emptied acolyte. He tore it away and fixed on the dark passage beyond the archive. “Before Deatholme closes around us.”
